The Sahel is one of the driest inhabited regions on Earth, yet its population is among the fastest-growing in the world. How does that arithmetic work?

Because population growth is driven by the gap between births and deaths, and in the Sahel that gap is the widest on Earth. Mortality — especially child mortality — has fallen with vaccines, malaria control, and better food logistics, while fertility remains very high: Niger's total fertility rate, around six to seven children per woman, is the world's highest. The result is growth near 3–4% a year, a doubling time of roughly twenty years, sustained by demographic momentum: even if fertility fell tomorrow, the huge cohorts of children already born would become parents. The land's carrying capacity, by contrast, is set by erratic rainfall on fragile soils, and it is not doubling. That scissors — people multiplying geometrically against a resource base that is static or degrading with climate change — is the central geographic tension of the region, driving migration south to the coastal cities and north toward the Mediterranean.
Why does Papua New Guinea have over 800 living languages — more than any other country — in a population of only about ten million?

Terrain chopped the population into isolates, and isolation manufactures languages. New Guinea's interior is a chaos of steep ridges, deep valleys, swamps, and dense forest where, before roads, the next valley might as well have been another continent. Small communities — often a few hundred people — lived for millennia in near-total separation, and languages drift apart fast in small groups: a few centuries of isolation yields mutual unintelligibility. Social structure reinforced it, since distinct languages marked group identity among neighbours who were trading partners and rivals at once. The same mechanism, at smaller scale, made the Caucasus the 'mountain of tongues' and kept pre-modern Europe a patchwork of dialects. Linguistic diversity maps are really maps of friction: where movement is easy — plains, rivers, empires — languages spread and merge; where the ground fights back, they multiply.
On most world maps Greenland looks about the same size as Africa. How wrong is that, and why?

Wrong by a factor of about fourteen: Africa is roughly 30.4 million km², Greenland about 2.2 million. The culprit is the Mercator projection (1569), which wraps the globe onto a cylinder and unrolls it. Mercator is conformal — it preserves angles and shapes locally, which made it superb for navigation, since a straight line on it is a constant compass bearing. The price is area: to keep angles true, scale inflates with latitude, so landmasses near the poles balloon. Greenland, straddling high latitudes, is inflated grotesquely; equatorial Africa barely grows. The distortion is a deliberate trade, not an error — but a classroom wall map that uses a navigator's projection to teach the sizes of countries teaches them wrongly, which is why geographers push equal-area projections for that job.
Why is north at the top of maps? Is there a physical reason?

None at all — it is a convention with a pedigree. The influential root is Ptolemy's Geography (2nd century CE), which oriented maps north-up in the Mediterranean tradition, and European mapmaking inherited it as printing spread. Other civilizations chose otherwise: many medieval European maps put east at the top (the rising sun, Eden) — which is why 'orientation' comes from oriens, Latin for east. Islamic maps often put south up, as did some Chinese maps, where the emperor faced south and subjects looked up at him from below. North won through a stack of reinforcing habits: the magnetic compass, the North Star as the navigator's fixed reference, and finally the sheer installed base of European charts. Australians have published 'upside-down' world maps since the 1970s to make the point: on a sphere floating in space, up is wherever you decide it is.
What does a map scale of 1:50,000 actually mean, and why can't a small-scale map just show everything in miniature?

1:50,000 means one unit on the map equals 50,000 of the same unit on the ground — one centimetre is 500 metres, one inch is about 0.8 miles. It is called a ratio or representative fraction, and it controls what can honestly be drawn. At 1:50,000 a road can be shown at something like its true width and individual buildings appear. Shrink to 1:5,000,000 and a city becomes a dot many times its real size while roads vanish — not because the cartographer is lazy, but because ink has width: a line 0.2 mm wide on a 1:5,000,000 map represents a kilometre on the ground. Small-scale maps therefore generalize — they select, simplify, and exaggerate — and every choice is an editorial act. This is the deep rule of cartography: a map at any scale is a model with deliberate omissions, and the scale tells you how aggressive the omissions must be.
Why can't anyone just make a perfectly accurate flat map of the Earth?

Because a sphere's surface and a plane are geometrically incompatible — you cannot flatten an orange peel without tearing or stretching it. Every projection is a choice of which properties to preserve and which to sacrifice among four: area, shape (angles), distance, and direction. Mercator keeps angles and sacrifices area; Gall–Peters keeps area and stretches shapes; azimuthal projections keep directions from one center point only. Mathematicians formalize the damage with Tissot's indicatrix — little circles drawn on the globe become ellipses of varying size and squish on the map, and no projection keeps them all as equal circles. Compromise projections like Robinson and Winkel Tripel preserve nothing exactly but distort everything only mildly, which is why atlases favor them. The impossibility is a theorem, not a technology gap: the only perfectly accurate map of Earth is a globe, and the only perfectly detailed one would be the size of the Earth itself.
What is the Gall–Peters projection, and why did it cause such a political argument?

Gall–Peters is an equal-area cylindrical projection — first described by James Gall in 1855 and promoted energetically by Arno Peters from 1973 — on which every country is drawn at its true relative size, correcting Mercator's inflation of the high latitudes. The cost is shape: landmasses are stretched vertically near the equator and compressed near the poles, so Africa and South America look long and thin. The argument was never really about geometry. Peters presented his map as an act of justice: Mercator, he argued, visually shrinks the developing world of the tropics and enlarges Europe, flattering the powerful. Critics replied that Mercator was designed for sailors, not propaganda, and that Peters's own map distorts shapes just as tendentiously. The durable lesson both sides proved is that every world map makes an argument — choosing a projection is choosing what truth to tell and what distortion to accept.
How do I read contour lines on a topographic map? What do close lines versus wide lines mean?

Each contour line joins points of equal elevation, so the pattern of lines is a picture of the land's shape. The rules that unlock it: closely spaced lines mean the elevation changes fast over a short horizontal distance — steep ground, a cliff or gorge wall. Widely spaced lines mean gentle slopes. Lines forming V shapes point uphill, toward higher ground, and the V's point upstream in a valley — water flows out of the V's mouth. Concentric closed loops are a hill or peak (the innermost loop is the top), unless marked with little hatch ticks, which indicate a depression. A saddle — the low pass between two peaks — shows as an hourglass pinch between two sets of loops. With those five rules you can read a landscape off paper: find the steep faces, the walkable ridges, and where the streams must run, before ever seeing the ground.
US election maps by state or county look overwhelmingly red, yet the national vote is nearly tied. What is the map doing to mislead?

It is mapping land, and land does not vote. A choropleth map fills each county or state with a color by winner, so visual weight is proportional to area — but electoral weight is proportional to people. The United States concentrates its population in a small share of its counties: the Los Angeles basin alone outvotes several Great Plains states combined, yet on the map it is a speck beside thousands of square kilometres of red farmland counties with a few thousand residents each. The eye integrates color by acreage and concludes a landslide. Cartographers fix this with cartograms — maps that resize each unit by population, so states swell or shrink to their electorate — or with dot-density and tile-grid maps where each state gets equal squares. The county map is not false; it answers 'who won the territory,' which is simply a different question from 'who won the people.'
Why does the prime meridian — 0 degrees longitude — run through Greenwich, London, of all places?

Politics and installed base, settled by vote. Latitude has a natural zero (the equator), but longitude's zero is arbitrary, and by the 19th century different countries used their own: Paris, Ferro in the Canaries, Washington, and others all appeared on charts. In 1884 the United States convened an International Meridian Conference in Washington, where 25 nations voted for a single prime meridian. Greenwich won because the practical argument was overwhelming: the majority of the world's shipping already navigated by British Admiralty charts and the Nautical Almanac, both keyed to Greenwich, and the Royal Observatory sat on the meridian with the transit instruments to define it. France, loyal to Paris, abstained and kept its own meridian on maps for decades. Zero longitude is in London for the same reason the QWERTY keyboard is under your fingers — not because it is optimal, but because it was already everywhere when the standard froze.
For over a century, European maps showed California as an island. How does an error that big survive that long?

Because early modern cartography ran on authority and copying, not verification. California was correctly drawn as a peninsula by early explorers, but a 1622 Dutch map — based on a Carmelite friar's report of a strait — redrew it as an island, and the striking image was copied by the great commercial map houses of Amsterdam, whose atlases set the standard everyone else traced. To correct it, a cartographer had to trust overland reports (the Jesuit Eusebio Kino walked the region and mapped the peninsula around 1700) over the printed consensus of famous firms — and publishers were reluctant to alter plates and contradict their own earlier editions. The error peaked in the mid-1600s and lingered on some maps into the 1700s, until a 1747 decree from Ferdinand VI of Spain declared California 'not an island' by royal order. The lesson survives in digital form: a plausible error, once embedded in the sources everyone copies, acquires the authority of consensus.
My GPS says one thing and an old survey map disagrees by a couple of metres. Why do coordinates themselves seem to move?

Because a coordinate is only meaningful relative to a datum — a mathematical model of the Earth's shape plus a fixed frame of reference points — and both the models and the ground move. Continents drift: Australia rides one of the fastest plates, moving northeast at about 7 cm a year, so its official datum of 1994 (GDA94) was roughly 1.8 metres out of alignment with global GPS coordinates by 2020, prompting a new datum, GDA2020, and plans for a time-dependent one. Older maps add their own offsets: datums fitted to a single country (like the old North American NAD27) can disagree with global WGS84 by hundreds of metres in places. GPS receivers report WGS84, which is periodically refined. So the 'same' latitude and longitude can legitimately point to different spots across datums — surveyors treat datum conversion as seriously as measurement itself, and a couple of metres of disagreement is usually not an error but two frames passing each other.
Why are time zone boundaries on maps so wiggly instead of following straight lines of longitude?

Because time zones are fitted to human geography, not imposed on it. A zone boundary that ran straight down a meridian would cut through cities, rail networks, and school districts, forcing neighbours onto different clocks. So boundaries detour around population: they follow state and national borders, bend to keep an island group or a metropolitan area whole, and bulge to include regions that trade with a distant capital — western China stays on Beijing time, and Spain's zone bulges an hour east of its sun. Even the number of zones is negotiable: France spans the most (twelve, counting overseas territories scattered across every ocean), while China uses one for five zones' worth of width. The wiggles are the visible signature of the real rule — clocks serve administration and commerce first, astronomy second.
What is the Winkel Tripel projection, and why did National Geographic adopt it for its world maps?

The Winkel Tripel (German for 'triple'), proposed by Oswald Winkel in 1921, is a compromise projection: it preserves no property exactly but keeps every distortion modest. It averages the coordinates of two older projections to soften both area and shape errors, and its curved meridians give the world an intuitively 'round' feel without the violent polar stretching of Mercator or the shape-squashing of equal-area cylindricals. National Geographic adopted it in 1998, replacing the Robinson projection it had used since 1988, after judging that Winkel Tripel had the lowest overall distortion for general-reference world maps — the kind used to show countries, oceans, and routes to lay readers. The choice is a philosophy statement: for a map meant to give an honest overall impression rather than serve navigation or area statistics, the best projection is the one that lies a little about everything instead of a lot about one thing.
London's Tube map famously distorts geography — stations' distances and directions are wrong. Why is it considered a design masterpiece anyway?

Because its job is not to depict London but to answer one question: how do I get from A to B on this network? Harry Beck, an engineering draughtsman, redrew the map in 1933 on the model of an electrical circuit diagram: lines run only horizontally, vertically, or at 45 degrees; stations are evenly spaced ticks; the tangled geography of central London is expanded and the suburbs compressed. What the map preserves perfectly is topology — the order of stations, the connections, where to change — which is exactly the information a rider needs and the only information they use underground, where real geography is invisible anyway. The geographic lies are the price of legibility, and every metro system on Earth now pays it gladly. Beck's map is the purest demonstration that a map's accuracy is not one thing: it can be geographically false and functionally true at the same time.
Why do 'upside-down' world maps with south at the top look so wrong, even though they're equally valid?

Because map reading is a learned reflex, and the learning is deep. By adulthood you have seen thousands of north-up maps; your sense of 'the shape of the world' is really the shape of that convention — the Americas' familiar silhouette, Australia tucked in its 'down under' corner (the phrase itself betrays the convention). Flip the map and pattern-matching fails: continents look unfamiliar, and places your brain files as 'remote south' suddenly loom at the top, which reads as importance. Nothing physical changes — on a globe in space there is no up. The disorientation is useful precisely because it exposes how much of what feels like geographic fact is cartographic habit. South-up maps, promoted in Australia since the 1970s, are less a correction than a diagnostic: they show you the moment your knowledge of the world turns out to be knowledge of a picture.
